title: Ikhfāʾ ḥaqīqī II — the hum takes its colour from what follows
objectives: Student can say whether an ikhfāʾ nasal is heavy or light before she says the phrase, from the following letter alone.
Student can produce the difference audibly on عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ against وَلَآ أَنتُمْ.
Student can read all fifteen letters cold, with the nasal intact on ف and ك.
Student can place an ikhfāʾ on the aʿlā / awsaṭ / adnā scale and say why the scale is descriptive, not three rulings.

slides.heading: Lesson 3.25 — Ikhfāʾ ḥaqīqī II: weight, degrees, and all fifteen letters
Two phrases she has memorised, and a question she will not expect
body: عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ (107:5) · وَلَآ أَنتُمْ (109:3). Both from sūrahs she has memorised. Both the same rule, taught last session.
Ask her to read both. Then ask: 'were those two hums the same sound?'
Almost every student says yes. They are not. Say them yourself, slowly, back to back, and let the difference sit in the air: the first hum is THICK and BACK, the second is THIN and FORWARD.
Same rule. Same two counts. Same tongue behaviour. Different WEIGHT — and the weight was decided by a letter that had not been pronounced yet.

Then the sentence that makes this lesson worth its own session: up to now, heavy and light have been properties of LETTERS. ص is heavy, ت is light; she learned that in 3-03 and has been applying it letter by letter ever since. Today heaviness stops being a property of a letter and becomes a property of a SOUND IN CONTEXT. The nasal has no weight of its own. It borrows one.
Name the error to come: she will flatten everything. Fifteen letters, one hum, no variation — because that is what she has been practising for a week and it was correct last lesson.

audio.cue: 107:5 — HEAVY. Thick, back. ص is an isti'lā letter.
109:3 — LIGHT. Thin, forward. ت is not. Same rule, opposite weight, and both are in her hifz.

slides.heading: Everything today is refinement of a rule she can already produce
body: 3-24 gave the rule, the fifteen letters, the couplet and the mechanism. Nothing today is new machinery; it is all one dial on a machine she already owns.

3-03 gave the isti'lā letters — خص ضغط قظ, the seven that raise the tongue. FIVE of them are among today's fifteen: ص ض ط ظ ق. The other two, خ and غ, are throat letters, so they belong to 3-20's rule instead.

3-07 gave tafkhīm and tarqīq in general, and taught that the alif INHERITS its weight from what PRECEDES it. Today's nasal inherits from what FOLLOWS. Same idea, opposite direction — say that out loud; it is the cleanest bridge available.
3-20 gave the distance explanation of the whole chapter. Today's three degrees are that same gradient, measured more finely.
So she does not need to memorise five more letters. She needs to understand one mechanism, and the list falls out of it.

slides.heading: The weight of the ikhfāʾ nasal
slides.condition: The nasal of ikhfāʾ adopts the heaviness of the letter it is running into. Heavy before ص ض ط ظ ق; light before the other ten.
body: Five heavy, ten light. The five heavy ones she already knows under another name: they are the isti'lā letters from 3-03, minus the two that live in the throat.
The other ten — ذ ث ك ج ش س د ز ف ت — take a thin, forward nasal.
The duration does not change. Two counts either way. Weight is not length, and a student who lengthens the heavy ones has confused two dials.
Nor does the ruling change: no shaddah on the following letter, tongue never at the noon's makhraj, exactly as last session.
One rule, one duration, two colours of sound.

slides.heading: Give the mechanism, not just the list — then the rule stops needing to be remembered
body: The tongue is ALREADY MOVING toward the next letter while the nasal runs. That was the whole mechanism of 3-24.
So if the next letter is one that raises the back of the tongue, the tongue is already raised WHILE SHE IS HUMMING.
The heaviness is not applied to the nasal. It is a physical consequence of where the tongue has already gone.
Have her feel it: hum toward a ص, and notice that the back of her tongue is up before the ص has been pronounced. Then hum toward a ت and notice that it is not.
Once she has felt that, the rule stops needing to be remembered. That is the difference between a list she will lose in a month and a mechanism she will keep.

Drill the pair before anything else: عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ / وَلَآ أَنتُمْ, ten times, alternating. Do not move on until she can hear it herself. If she cannot hear it, she cannot check herself at home, and the rest of the lesson is decoration.

slides.heading: The three degrees — and what the scale is for, because it is easy to misuse
body: The nearer the following letter's makhraj is to the noon's, the closer the ikhfāʾ sits to a merge.
AʿLĀ — closest to idghām: ط · د · ت. Their makhraj is almost on the noon's own.
AWSAṬ — middle: the remaining eleven. The default sound.
ADNĀ — closest to iẓhār: ق · ك. The furthest makhraj; the noon is barely veiled.
These are NOT three different rulings. All three are a 2-count nasal with no shaddah. The scale is DESCRIPTIVE, and its use is DIAGNOSTIC.

A student whose مِن قَبْلُ sounds like iẓhār and whose أَنتُمْ sounds like idghām is not making two errors. She is exaggerating a real gradient. That one sentence will save you from mis-correcting her at least twice this month — and tell HER too, because a learner who has been told her مِن قَبْلُ sounds 'too plain' needs to know the letter is genuinely near that end of the scale.

audio.cue: 109:3 — ت, AʿLĀ. Nearest to a merge. If it doubles, look at the page: where is the shaddah?
2:25 — reference example, outside your memorised sūrahs. ق, ADNĀ. Nearly plain is not plain; the tongue still must not touch.

slides.translation: Those who are heedless of their prayer.

audio.cue: 107:5 — the heavy anchor. هُمْ عَن is an iẓhār shafawī from 3-18; عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ is today's rule with a thick, back nasal. One of only two heavy ikhfāʾs available to her inside the hifz set, so drill it rather than a reference.

slides.translation: Nor are you worshippers of what I worship.

audio.cue: 109:3 — the light anchor, and the aʿlā end of the degree scale at the same time. أَنتُمْ, inside one word, thin forward nasal. She meets it again in 109:5 word for word — two identical instances in one sūrah, and she takes 109:1–3 as today's Sabaq.

slides.heading: The six letters she can check against her own memory
body: Six of the fifteen have an instance inside her memorised sūrahs. Lean the drilling on these; they are worth several she cannot verify.
ص — عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ, 107:5. HEAVY, awsaṭ.
ذ — نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ, 111:3. Light, awsaṭ, and on a tanwīn.
ج — مِّن جُوعٍ, 106:4. Light, awsaṭ. The anchor from last session.
ش — مِن شَرِّ, 113:2. Light, awsaṭ. Five instances across al-Falaq and an-Nās.
س — مِّن سِجِّيلٍ, 105:4. Light, awsaṭ.
ت — وَلَآ أَنتُمْ, 109:3. Light, AʿLĀ, and inside one word.

audio.cue: 111:3 — ذ, light. A tanwīn, not a written noon.
113:2 — ش, light. The most-repeated instance she owns.

slides.heading: The nine she cannot — reference examples, outside your memorised sūrahs
body: Nine of the fifteen letters have no in-set instance, and that is simply what the hifz set contains. Do not hide the imbalance; say which rows she can check against her own memory and which she cannot.
ث — مِن ثَمَرَةٍ, 2:25. Light. · ك — مِّن كُلِّ أَمْرٍ, 97:4. Light, ADNĀ.
ق — مِن قَبْلُ, 2:25. HEAVY, ADNĀ. · د — مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ, 2:23. Light, AʿLĀ.
ط — مِّن طِينٍ, 6:2. HEAVY, AʿLĀ. · ز — إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَٰهُ, 97:1. Light.
ف — أَنفُسَهُمْ, 2:9. Light. · ض — مِّن ضَعْفٍ, 30:54. HEAVY. · ظ — ظِلًّا ظَلِيلًا, 4:57. HEAVY, on a tanwīn.

ظِلًّا ظَلِيلًا is worth using even though it is a reference: a tanwīn running into a ظ, and the ظ is one of the heaviest letters in the language. It is the clearest heavy nasal available. Say it, then say وَلَآ أَنتُمْ — the two extremes of the weight scale, back to back.

إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَٰهُ is worth its own thirty seconds for a different reason: a DOUBLED noon and a CONCEALED noon two words apart. Both hum for two counts. In the first the tongue is firmly on the gum ridge for the whole hold; in the second it never goes there at all. Same duration, opposite tongue. If she can do both in one breath, the chapter is working.

audio.cue: 4:57 — reference example. The heaviest nasal available anywhere. Tanwīn + ظ.
97:1 — reference example. Doubled noon, then concealed noon. Same length, opposite tongue.
6:2 — reference example. ط, heavy AND aʿlā. Both scales at once.

slides.heading: The two that decay first, and the two that get fused
body: ف and ك. The join into them is comfortable without a nasal, so nothing in the mouth forces the issue and nothing in the ear complains.
أَنفُسَهُمْ and مِّن كُلِّ أَمْرٍ will lose their hum before any other row in the table — not this week, but in a month, quietly.
Put them on the weekly maintenance list NOW, before they decay, rather than rediscovering them later. This is the one item from today that never comes off the list.
Then close the loop on ق and ك. They are both ADNĀ — nearest to iẓhār — and ق is HEAVY while ك is LIGHT. The two facts are independent, and students routinely fuse them into 'adnā letters are heavy'.
مِن قَبْلُ and مِّن كُلِّ أَمْرٍ back to back settles it: same degree, opposite weight. Five times, and the fusion does not survive.

audio.cue: 2:9 — reference example. ف, light. Pinch it: the nose must block for two counts.
97:4 — reference example. ك, light, adnā. Pinch it too.
16:112 — reference example. A second ك for the maintenance drill.

slides.heading: Same rule, same length, three different sounds

pairs.note: HEAVY, awsaṭ. Thick and back, because the tongue is already raised for the ص while the nasal is still running. In her hifz.
LIGHT, aʿlā. Thin and forward — and nearest of all fifteen to a merge. Same violet on the page as the row above, same two counts, and a completely different sound. In her hifz.
HEAVY, adnā. Nearest to an iẓhār — so the concealment is genuinely lightest here — and heavy at the same time. The two scales are independent. Reference example — outside your memorised sūrahs.

slides.heading: One key for all fifteen letters, at every weight and every degree
Colour, one honest note
body: Everything on today's table is the same violet, #9400A8, cpfair key ikhfa.
The colour does not tell her the WEIGHT and does not tell her the DEGREE. The page marks THAT a concealment happens, not HOW it sounds.
This is the general limit of colour-coding and it is worth saying once, plainly: the colours locate rules; they do not execute them.
It is the same admission she got in 3-21 about kāmil and nāqiṣ sharing one teal, and in 3-22 about the two greens. Three lessons, one lesson about colour: it is an index, not an instruction set.

And prepare next session while the table is still on the board. 3-26 puts all four noon rules in one drill and proves the partition — 6 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 15 = 28. Tell her the arithmetic is coming, and ask her to work out for herself, before then, why it HAS to add to 28.

slides.heading: The weight pair — before anything else
slides.instructions: Ten times, alternating, listening to the HUM and not to the letters. Do not move on until she can hear it herself. If she cannot hear it, record both and play them back.

slides.heading: Call the weight first — and the two extremes
slides.instructions: Someone reads a letter from the fifteen. Say 'heavy' or 'light' BEFORE you are shown a phrase. Then read the phrase. Twenty repetitions, random order. Then the two extremes, five times back to back — if those two sound the same, nothing in this lesson has landed yet and you start again at the weight pair.

audio.cue: The five heavy. Isti'lā from 3-03, minus خ and غ which are throat letters.

grid.arabic: ذ · ث · ك · ج · ش · س · د · ز · ف · ت

audio.cue: The ten light. Ten of fifteen — heavy is the exception, not the reward.
97:4 — adnā, LIGHT. Same degree, opposite weight. Five times, and the fusion does not survive.

slides.heading: The decay list — ف and ك, with the pinch
slides.instructions: The nose must block for two counts on every one. Put this drill in your weekly maintenance permanently; it is the one item from today that never comes off the list.

slides.heading: Same length, opposite tongue
slides.instructions: Say each pair. Both hum for two counts; only the left one puts the tongue on the gum ridge. If she can do both in one breath, the chapter is working.

audio.cue: 110:3 — doubled noon. Tongue ON the ridge for the whole hold. 3-15.
114:4 — concealed noon, four words earlier in the same ayah. Never arrives.
97:1 — reference example. Both in one phrase, two words apart. The cleanest demonstration available.

slides.heading: The whole chapter, mixed
slides.instructions: Read down and name the rule. Four rules in play; do not think, answer. Teacher key, in order: ikhfāʾ · iẓhār · idghām with ghunnah ×2 · iqlāb · ikhfāʾ heavy · iẓhār · ikhfāʾ heavy · idghām without ghunnah · iẓhār · idghām without ghunnah · idghām with ghunnah nāqiṣ · ikhfāʾ light.

audio.cue: 107:4 — idghām without ghunnah, on a tanwīn.
2:8 — reference example. Idghām with ghunnah, nāqiṣ.
2:9 — reference example. Ikhfāʾ, light, and the hum is the thing that goes missing.

slides.heading: In the sūrahs, naming as you go
slides.instructions: Recite al-Māʿūn, al-Kāfirūn and al-Falaq from memory, naming every noon rule out loud as you pass it, mid-recitation. It will sound ridiculous. It is the single best preparation for next session, and it is the only exercise that catches correct weight in the drill and flat weight in the sūrah.

audio.cue: 107:5 — iẓhār shafawī, then a heavy ikhfāʾ. Two chapters in five words.
109:3 — today's Sabaq, and the same words again as 109:5. Light ikhfāʾ, twice in one sūrah.
114:4 — light ikhfāʾ, then a doubled noon. Same length, opposite tongue, inside one line she recites daily.

slides.heading: The seven things that go wrong

mistakes.wrong: One flat hum for all fifteen letters — عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ and وَلَآ أَنتُمْ sounding identical.
mistakes.why: She spent a week building one reliable nasal, and it was correct last lesson. Now she is being asked to vary it. This is a direct consequence of 3-24 doing its job.
mistakes.fix: The weight pair and the two extremes. Alternate; do not explain. If she cannot hear the difference between the extremes, record both and play them back. Priority error of the lesson.

mistakes.wrong: Heaviness leaking onto light letters — a thick hum before ت, س, ش.
mistakes.why: Over-correction, usually in the session right after you fix the flat hum. Heavy sounds impressive.
mistakes.fix: 'Ten of the fifteen are light. Heavy is the exception, not the reward.'

mistakes.wrong: The nasal disappearing on ف and ك.
mistakes.why: The join is comfortable without it and the ear does not object. It will not happen today; it happens in a month, quietly.
mistakes.fix: The pinch drill on أَنفُسَهُمْ and مِّن كُلِّ, on the weekly maintenance list permanently.

mistakes.wrong: Turning مِن قَبْلُ into a full iẓhār — an audible noon before the ق.
mistakes.why: ق is adnā, genuinely close to iẓhār, so she is exaggerating a real gradient rather than inventing an error.
mistakes.fix: 'Nearly plain is not plain. The tongue still does not touch.' Correct it gently and SAY that it is a real gradient.

mistakes.wrong: Turning أَنتُمْ into a merge — a doubled ت.
mistakes.why: ت is aʿlā, genuinely close to idghām. The same phenomenon as the ق error, at the other end of the scale.
mistakes.fix: 'Where is the shaddah?' Look at the page.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the three degrees as three rules — three different durations, or a question like 'how long is the adnā one?'.
mistakes.why: A table with three rows looks like three rulings.
mistakes.fix: 'All three are two counts and no shaddah. The scale describes the COLOUR of the sound, not the ruling.'

mistakes.wrong: Losing the weight rule inside a full recitation — correct weight in the drill, flat weight in the sūrah.
mistakes.why: A rule applied under drill conditions has not yet been applied under reading conditions. Very common, and the drill will not reveal it.
mistakes.fix: Name rules mid-recitation, out loud, on al-Māʿūn, al-Kāfirūn and al-Falaq. That is what moves a rule from the exercise into the text.

slides.heading: One rule, one duration, two weights, three degrees

audio.cue: HEAVY. ص ض ط ظ ق — five letters, and she already knew them as isti'lā.
LIGHT. The other ten. Heavy is the exception, not the reward.
Adnā and heavy at once. The two scales are independent; do not fuse them.
The hum that goes missing first. Pinch it weekly, forever. Next session: 6 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 15 = 28 — work out before then why it HAS to add to 28.

slides.heading: Homework — 15–20 min/day, five days
tasks: Two minutes — the weight pair, alternating. Every day.
Three minutes — the full fifteen-letter table, weight named out loud BEFORE each phrase. Once slowly, then once at pace.
Two minutes — ف and ك with the pinch. This one never comes off the list.
Two minutes — the two extremes; then same degree, opposite weight (مِن قَبْلُ against مِّن كُلِّ أَمْرٍ).
Two minutes — same length, opposite tongue. Doubled noon against concealed noon, in one breath.
Four minutes — the mixed column, cold, naming the rule with no pause.
Three minutes — al-Māʿūn, al-Kāfirūn and al-Falaq from memory, naming rules as you pass them.

The rest — hifz. Manzil run consecutively, Sabqi (110 whole, now complete, plus whatever is still recent), then the new Sabaq al-Kāfirūn 109:1–3 with FORTY repetitions rather than twenty. Bring to the next session: the four noon rules, their letter counts, and the total.

script: Open with two phrases she has memorised — عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ and وَلَآ أَنتُمْ — and a question she will not expect: 'were those two hums the same sound?' Almost every student says yes. Then say them yourself, slowly, back to back, and let the difference sit in the air.

Then the sentence that earns this session: up to now heavy and light have been properties of LETTERS. Today heaviness becomes a property of a SOUND IN CONTEXT. The nasal has no weight of its own; it borrows one from a letter that has not been pronounced yet.
Name the error before it arrives: she will flatten everything. Fifteen letters, one hum — because that is what she practised all week and it was correct last lesson.

Bridge to 3-07 explicitly: the alif inherits its weight from what PRECEDES it; today's nasal inherits from what FOLLOWS. Same idea, opposite direction. It is the cleanest bridge available and it costs one sentence.

Give the mechanism rather than the list. The tongue is already moving toward the next letter while the nasal runs — that was 3-24's whole mechanism. If the next letter raises the back of the tongue, the tongue is already raised while she is humming. Have her FEEL it: hum toward a ص, notice the back of the tongue is up. Once she has felt that, the rule stops needing to be remembered.

Drill the pair before anything else, ten times alternating. Do not move on until she can hear it herself — if she cannot hear it she cannot check herself at home, and everything after this is decoration.

Then the three degrees, and immediately say what the classification is FOR, because it is easy to misuse. These are not three rulings. All three are two counts and no shaddah. The scale is descriptive and its use is diagnostic: a student whose مِن قَبْلُ sounds like iẓhār and whose أَنتُمْ sounds like idghām is not making two errors, she is exaggerating a real gradient. That sentence will save you from mis-correcting her twice this month — and tell HER, so she knows the letters are genuinely near those ends.

Run all fifteen letters systematically; this is the consolidation the lesson exists for. Six have an in-set instance — ص ذ ج ش س ت — and nine do not. Do not hide the imbalance. Say which rows she can check against her own memory and which she cannot, and lean the drilling on the six.

ظِلًّا ظَلِيلًا earns its place as a reference: a tanwīn into a ظ, one of the heaviest letters in the language, and the clearest heavy nasal available anywhere. Say it, then وَلَآ أَنتُمْ — the two extremes back to back.

إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَٰهُ is worth thirty seconds for the opposite reason: a doubled noon and a concealed noon two words apart. Both hum for two counts; in the first the tongue is on the ridge for the whole hold, in the second it never goes there. Same duration, opposite tongue. If she can do both in one breath, the chapter is working.

Flag ف and ك and give them their own minute. The join is comfortable without a nasal, so nothing forces the issue and nothing in the ear complains. They will lose their hum in a month, quietly. Put them on the weekly maintenance list NOW rather than rediscovering them later.
Close the loop on ق and ك: both adnā, and ق heavy while ك light. Students fuse the two facts into 'adnā means heavy'. مِن قَبْلُ against مِّن كُلِّ أَمْرٍ, five times, settles it.

Colour, one honest note: everything on today's table is the same violet, #9400A8. The colour does not tell her the weight and does not tell her the degree. The page marks THAT a concealment happens, not HOW it sounds. Say it once, plainly — the colours locate rules; they do not execute them. It is the third lesson running to make that admission.

Prepare 3-26 while the table is still up. The arithmetic 6 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 15 = 28 is coming, and ask her to work out for herself, before then, why it HAS to add to 28. Arriving at the answer herself is worth more than being shown it.

Hifz: Manzil run consecutively. Sabqi — an-Naṣr 110 now complete, three ayat, plus 111 and 112 if either is still in the recent window; promote whatever has come back clean three sessions running. New Sabaq al-Kāfirūn 109:1–3, three ayat in one session and deliberately so: al-Kāfirūn is the most repetitive sūrah in the hifz set, ayat 3 and 5 are word-for-word identical, and the commonest error is not forgetting a line but reciting the right line in the wrong place. Give it forty repetitions rather than twenty. وَلَآ أَنتُمْ in 109:3 is today's light anchor, and she meets it again in 109:5.

listenFor.correctionCue: Naming rules out loud mid-recitation on al-Māʿūn, al-Kāfirūn and al-Falaq. It sounds ridiculous and it is what moves a rule from the exercise into the text.

teacherNotes.homework: 15–20 min/day, five days. Daily: two minutes on the weight pair, alternating, listening to the hum and not the letters; three minutes down the full fifteen-letter table with the weight named out loud before each phrase, once slowly and once at pace; two minutes on ف and ك with the pinch, which never comes off the list; two minutes on the two extremes (ظِلًّا ظَلِيلًا against وَلَآ أَنتُمْ) and then same degree opposite weight (مِن قَبْلُ against مِّن كُلِّ أَمْرٍ); two minutes on same length, opposite tongue — a doubled noon and a concealed noon in one breath; four minutes on the mixed column cold, naming the rule with no pause; three minutes reciting al-Māʿūn, al-Kāfirūn and al-Falaq from memory while naming rules mid-recitation. Hifz: Manzil run consecutively, Sabqi (an-Naṣr 110 now complete, plus anything still recent, with promotion for whatever has come back clean three sessions running), then the new Sabaq al-Kāfirūn 109:1–3 at forty repetitions rather than twenty — the sūrah's repetitiveness makes it feel easier than it is, and the commonest error is reciting the right line in the wrong place. She brings to the next session the four noon rules, their letter counts, and the total.
